abstract: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent’s acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent’s own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet’s. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.

sections.body: The paper starts from the standard model of collective motion, in which social forces act between pairs of individuals. It cites evidence of three-body contributions in golden shiners, and notes that the neural model SocialNet mixes all body orders in one nonlinear aggregation. It adapts the atomic cluster expansion from atomic physics to self-propelled agents, producing the directional atomic cluster expansion, dACE. Tests cover simulated collectives with known 2-, 3- and 4-body rules, tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, and SocialNet, which is compared in 2D only. An open-source Julia implementation is released.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Pairwise models miss many-body effects, so the paper adapts a body-ordered atomic expansion to self-propelled agents.

sections.body: The section defines the atomic cluster expansion, a body-ordered expansion of functions of neighbour sets. Products of pooled features are replaced by a purification step, so each body order's coefficients are uniquely identified. The directional version gives each neighbour a relative position and a relative velocity, and uses a single joint rotation symmetry, so the expansion is exactly equivariant. The self term depends on the agent's past motion and is fitted after the interaction terms, on their residual, so it does not absorb them. Coefficients come from regularised least squares, with the regularisation chosen by maximising marginal likelihood, and the solver streams data in chunks. The software is implemented in Julia.
sections.heading: Directional atomic cluster expansion
sections.headline: The directional expansion writes an agent's acceleration as pure body-ordered terms plus a separate self term.

sections.body: Tests use D'Orsogna-type self-propelled particles with alignment, plus 2-, 3- and 4-body rules whose body order is known, and two discontinuous classical models, Boids and a zonal model. Error is the relative force error on held-out environments. Each model's error drops once its body order reaches the rule's, and a 2-body model fails on every many-body rule. dACE needs less data than SocialNet, whose error improves slowly with more samples. Limits: the discontinuous Boids and zonal rules keep error large for every model. Next-step prediction accuracy rises with self-propulsion, even as the learned force gets worse.
sections.heading: Numerical experiments on synthetic data
sections.headline: On simulated rules with known body order, dACE recovers each term and needs less data than SocialNet.

sections.body: The zebrafish data are eight videos of groups of 60 to 100 fish, and the golden shiner data are ten trials of groups of 10 to 151 fish. A 3-body dACE model with a staged self term is fitted and tested by leaving one video or trial out. For zebrafish with no skipped frames, adding interactions raises R² from 10.5 to 11.9 percent, and the 3-body model beats the 2-body model on every shiner trial. Laws fitted to disjoint halves of the data agree better for dACE than for SocialNet, and with 1000 samples per half SocialNet's two laws disagree by more than their own size. SocialNet gains more from interactions on zebrafish, but from a far weaker self model, so that gain does not indicate better interactions.
sections.heading: Numerical experiments on tracking data
sections.headline: On tracked fish, dACE's learned laws are generally more consistent between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's.

sections.body: Data can show whether pairwise interactions suffice: the higher-order terms are negligible for pairwise rules and large for the others. Next-step accuracy rose in simulations while the learned interactions got worse, so it is a poor guide to interaction models. The paper recommends several checks together: prediction under a protocol with no shared frames, the gain from adding interactions, and consistency between disjoint data sets. Open directions include neighbourhoods defined by selection or occlusion, obstacles and other species as particle types, and piecewise polynomial bases for hard-zone rules, whose knots must be known or learned.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Data can show whether pairwise rules suffice, and next-step accuracy alone is a poor guide to interaction models.
